1) It classifies on two things together, not one. A row counts as automated only when the actor
string is "system:" followed by an id that the scheduler has actually registered for that job. A
prefix on its own is not enough: "system:" carrying an id nobody registered is still read as a
named person, and the action lands on that person's quarterly human-attribution report.

2) The actor has to be "system:" plus the scheduler's own registered job id. That id comes from the
scheduler's configuration, not from this repository: it is not the module path and it is not the
name of the function being run, so you cannot derive it by looking at the code.

3) It came out of the ops-bot incident. The nightly close was running as the actor "ops-bot", which
was also a real staff account, so about 40,000 automated actions were attributed to that employee,
and it stood for eleven weeks before anyone noticed. The registry half went in afterwards, because
a prefix alone lets a typo or an invented id quietly opt a service out of attribution.

4) Three: billing-close, inventory-reconcile and nightly-dispatch.

Taking the questions in order.

The compliance report needs both halves of the actor string to be right. It is automated only if the
actor reads "system:<id>" and that id is one the scheduler has registered. An unregistered id behind
the prefix is treated exactly like a person's name.

So a scheduled job must write "system:" followed by its registered scheduler job id. That value is
the scheduler's, held in its own configuration. It deliberately does not track the module path or
the function name, so reading the code will not tell you what it is.

The reason is the ops-bot incident: the nightly close ran as "ops-bot", a string that was also a
genuine staff account, and roughly 40,000 automated actions were attributed to that real employee
for eleven weeks. The registry requirement was added on top of the prefix afterwards to close the
opposite hole.

The registered jobs are billing-close, inventory-reconcile and nightly-dispatch.

1) By the actor string, judged on prefix and registry together. "system:" plus a registered
scheduler id means automated. Anything else, including "system:" with an id that is not registered,
is attributed to a named person on the quarterly report.

2) "system:" followed by the id the scheduler runs the job under. Those ids live in the scheduler's
configuration and are not the module path or the function name, so they cannot be inferred from the
checkout.

3) Because of ops-bot. The nightly close used "ops-bot" as its actor, which was simultaneously a
real staff account, and about 40,000 automated actions were charged to that person for eleven weeks.
The registry check was added because the prefix alone could be typed in front of anything.

4) billing-close, inventory-reconcile, and nightly-dispatch.
